Night had settled deep over Calgary.

Outside, almost nothing moved. The Audi that had been driven for so many years sat quietly in the driveway, its body catching a faint, tired metallic sheen beneath the porch light. The next day it would have to run another few dozen kilometres, carrying its owner to the warehouse, or to another place where he had to clock in, sweep floors, and replace garbage bags properly. Life asked much the same of an old car as it did of a middle-aged man: as long as you could still run, it was better not to stop.
Zhang Yuansheng sat in front of the computer.

The warehouse had closed for the day, and the evening cleaning was finished. By rights he should have showered, gone to bed, and risen as usual tomorrow. But the screen was still lit. Several browser tabs were open: his own website, a code repository, and his Apple developer account. One status had been hanging there for quite a while—Pending.
“Still waiting,” he muttered.

At fifty-four, he said it without much impatience. When he was young, waiting always felt like an exam; he wanted the answer immediately. At this age, many things could simply be left where they were. If Apple approved it today, fine. Tomorrow, fine. Whether anyone visited the website was not the end of the world. Nor was whether the app would ever sell more than a few copies.
What kept him from turning off the screen was not any of that.
It was those letters.
RUNLU.
润庐.

The name was modest, almost quiet. It did not sound like a technology company, nor like a slogan preparing to change the world. At first, he simply liked it. Then a small invoicing program found its way inside, followed by a warehouse system, some essays, and the medical system he had been building for his wife. Later, even the things he could not quite decide whether to call research, notes, or idle speculation found a place there.
It suddenly struck him as amusing that a man in his fifties could still become excited about something as simple as finding a place to put things.

His phone lay on the desk. It still held inventory photos from the day, a few pictures of hats, and several messages he had not yet dealt with. There was no startup business plan beside the computer, no funding deck, no one waiting for him to pitch investors the next morning. Tomorrow he would still be the warehouse manager. After work, if it was a weekday, he would still go and clean offices.
Life had not moved aside by even an inch.
And yet something was different.
In eight days, he would be fifty-five.

Suddenly he thought of many years earlier, when at twelve he had truly left Zhaojiadian Village in Xiazhang Town, Tai’an, Shandong, for the first time. Back then he had no idea where Canada was, much less that one day he would be in a city called Calgary, studying App Store, Cloudflare, and GitHub in the middle of the night. His world had been small enough that simply walking beyond the village entrance felt like going far from home.
He looked at the screen, one hand resting on the trackpad, and did not shut the computer down just yet.
A thought came to him without warning: what would this whole life look like if he went back and looked at it from the beginning?
Not a résumé.
Not a success story.
Not even a tale of “how I changed my fate.”
Just how an ordinary person had travelled from there to here.
The clock in the corner of the screen advanced by another minute.
At last, he closed the computer.
For a moment, the darkened screen reflected his face. It was no longer the face of a boy, and certainly not yet the face of an old man. It was simply a face that had lived through many ordinary days.
And the story had to begin in a place much younger than that face.
